paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared
paragraphs.mainIdea: A magic tree house appears in the woods of a small town.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day, a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.

background.note: Frog Creek is a made-up small town. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the United States.

paragraphs.context: They visited dinosaurs, knights, an Egyptian queen
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us about Jack and Annie's first trips.
paragraphs.simple: Before this book, the tree house took Jack and Annie to the time of the dinosaurs, to knights and castles, to ancient Egypt, to pirates, to ninjas in old Japan, and to the Amazon rain forest. Each trip is a different book in the series.

background.note: A queen of ancient Egypt, more than 3,000 years ago.
A very big, hot, wet forest in South America.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, they discovered that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie learned that the tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She can do magic, and she travels to different times and places to collect books.

background.note: A woman who can do magic in the old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is kind and loves books.
A king in old British stories. He and his knights lived in a castle called Camelot.

paragraphs.context: One day, Jack and Annie found a note that said Morgan was under a spell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is in trouble, and Jack and Annie must find four special things to help her.
paragraphs.simple: Someone has put magic on Morgan, and she is not free. Jack and Annie must find four special things to help her.

paragraphs.context: With the help of a mouse named Peanut
paragraphs.mainIdea: They already have three of the four special things.
paragraphs.simple: A mouse called Peanut helped them. They found the first thing in old Japan, the second in the Amazon rain forest and the third in the Ice Age. Now only one thing is left.

background.note: A time long ago when ice covered much of the earth. People hunted mammoths then.

paragraphs.context: Annie was right, thought Jack. The moon was so bright
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moonlight is very bright tonight.
paragraphs.simple: The moon was so bright that Jack could see his own shadow. Everything looked silver in the light.
paragraphs.tone: "Washed with silver" is a beautiful picture: the light seems to cover everything like silver paint. It makes the night feel quiet and magic.

paragraphs.context: It shone on the three M things that rested on the M
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moonlight shines on the three special things they found before.
paragraphs.simple: The moonlight fell on the three things on the letter M: a moonstone from the ninja trip, a mango from the rain forest and a mammoth bone from the Ice Age. All three start with M.

paragraphs.context: There’s no air. We couldn’t breathe
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains why people can't just go to the moon.
paragraphs.simple: There is no air on the moon, so you can't breathe. It is also terribly hot in the daytime and terribly cold at night.
paragraphs.tone: Jack sounds like a little teacher. He likes facts.

paragraphs.context: Maybe a place where people train to be astronauts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the picture may show a place for training astronauts.
paragraphs.simple: Jack guesses the picture shows a place on Earth where people learn to be astronauts. He doesn't believe they will really go to the moon.

background.note: People who travel into space. Before a trip, they train for years on Earth.

paragraphs.context: A moon base was built on the moon in the year 2031
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says there is a moon base in the year 2031.
paragraphs.simple: The book says people built a base on the moon in 2031. Spaceships come in and go out through a door at the top of the round roof.

background.note: This book was written in 1996, so 2031 was the future. It is a made-up date in the story.

paragraphs.context: The book says the moon base was built in the year 2031
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack understands that the book comes from the future.
paragraphs.simple: If the book tells about something built in 2031, it must have been written after 2031. So the book is from the future!
paragraphs.tone: Jack is very excited. He thinks it through like a detective.

paragraphs.context: The small base has a landing chamber and a room for storing spacesuits
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells what is inside the moon base.
paragraphs.simple: The base has a room where spaceships land and a room for spacesuits. Machines give air and keep the temperature right, so people can breathe.

paragraphs.context: He stared at a rocky gray land
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees the moon's land and its strange black sky.
paragraphs.simple: The land is gray and full of rocks, big holes and high mountains. The sun is shining, but the sky is black, not blue.

background.note: On Earth, air makes the daytime sky look blue. The moon has no air, so its sky is black even when the sun is shining.

paragraphs.context: It takes fourteen Earth days to equal one day on the moon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daytime on the moon is very long and very hot.
paragraphs.simple: One day on the moon is as long as fourteen days on Earth. There is no air to protect the moon from the sun, so in the daytime it gets as hot as 260 degrees.

background.note: 260 degrees Fahrenheit, the American way to measure heat. It is about 127 degrees Celsius, hotter than boiling water.

paragraphs.context: Moon scientists wear spacesuits, which have controls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Spacesuits keep the scientists safe.
paragraphs.simple: The spacesuits can make the person inside warmer or cooler. Their tanks give air for two hours.
paragraphs.tone: "Two hours" is important: Jack and Annie only have two hours of air.

paragraphs.context: Wow, it’s like the armor room in a castle
paragraphs.mainIdea: The spacesuits remind Jack of knights' armor.
paragraphs.simple: The row of spacesuits looks like a castle room full of knights' metal suits.

background.term: the armor room in a castle
background.note: In their second trip, Jack and Annie visited a castle with knights. Knights wore metal suits called armor.

paragraphs.context: Ow! Talk quietly,” Jack said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie talks too loudly in her helmet.
paragraphs.simple: There are radios inside the helmets, so they can hear each other well. Annie doesn't need to shout.

paragraphs.context: Ready?” said Annie. “Open sesame!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says magic words as she opens the door.
paragraphs.simple: Annie presses the button and says "Open sesame!" One door closes behind them and another opens in front of them.

background.note: Magic words from the old story "Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves". In the story, these words open a secret cave. Annie says them for fun.

paragraphs.context: The moon has no rain or wind to blow the dust around
paragraphs.mainIdea: Footprints on the moon stay there forever.
paragraphs.simple: On Earth, wind and rain soon wipe away footprints. The moon has no rain or wind, so footprints can stay there for a billion years.

paragraphs.context: For the first time, it really hit Jack
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack suddenly understands that they are really in space.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack sees the Earth far away, he suddenly really feels it: they are in outer space!
paragraphs.tone: Short sentences ("Earth.") show that Jack is so surprised he can hardly think.

paragraphs.context: I’m a moon rabbit
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie jumps around like a rabbit.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is hopping across the moon, so she calls herself a moon rabbit.

background.note: In many Asian stories, people see a rabbit in the dark marks on the moon. In the Chinese story, the rabbit lives on the moon with Chang'e. Annie is just playing, but the idea is very old.

paragraphs.context: A person weighs less on the moon because of the moon’s low gravity
paragraphs.mainIdea: You are much lighter on the moon.
paragraphs.simple: The moon pulls things down much less than the Earth does. So you weigh only one sixth as much there.

background.note: About 27 kilograms.
About 4.5 kilograms.

paragraphs.context: But you don’t have a license!” said Jack
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie jokes that she doesn't need a license on the moon.
paragraphs.simple: There are no roads, traffic lights or police on the moon, so Annie says nobody will stop her from driving.
paragraphs.tone: This is a funny moment. Annie is only seven, and she is happy to break the rules.

background.note: In the US you must be 16 or older and pass a test to get a driver's license.

paragraphs.context: Annie steered the buggy over the tracks on the ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: The buggy is made for the moon's deep dust.
paragraphs.simple: Annie drives over the marks in the dust. The buggy's wide wheels stop it from going down into the soft dust.

paragraphs.context: Annie drove the moon buggy over bumps and hollows
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ride is very bumpy.
paragraphs.simple: The buggy goes up and down over the uneven ground. It jumps like a wild horse.

background.note: A wild horse that jumps and kicks to throw off its rider. People ride broncos at a rodeo, a cowboy show.

paragraphs.context: Look for the fo-fourth M thing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie can hardly talk on the bumpy ride.
paragraphs.simple: Annie bounces so much that her words get broken up.
paragraphs.tone: "Fo-fourth" is written that way to show her voice shaking on the bumpy ride. Later you see "Sl-slow d-down" and "b-brake" for the same reason.

paragraphs.context: He had never been to such a colorless, barren place
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moon has no color and no life.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has never seen a place with no colors and nothing growing at all. Everything is gray.
paragraphs.tone: The short list "no green, no blue, no red" makes the moon feel empty and lonely.

paragraphs.context: That’s from the first astronauts who landed on the moon
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find the place where people first landed on the moon.
paragraphs.simple: The American flag was left by the first astronauts on the moon.

background.term: the first astronauts who landed on the moon
background.note: In July 1969, the American spaceship Apollo 11 landed on the moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to walk there.

paragraphs.context: HERE MEN FROM THE PLANET
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sign left by the first astronauts on the moon.
paragraphs.simple: The sign says: People from Earth first walked on the moon here in July 1969. We came as friends, for all people.
paragraphs.tone: The words on the real sign are written on separate lines. In this book the line breaks are lost, so you see "EARTHFIRST" and "PEACEFOR". Read them as "EARTH / FIRST" and "PEACE / FOR".

background.note: "Anno Domini", Latin words. It is used with years after the birth of Jesus, like 1969.
All people in the world.

paragraphs.context: It would be there forever, unless someone moved it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their names will stay on the moon forever.
paragraphs.simple: Nothing on the moon will blow away or wash away their names. Only a person could move the notebook.
paragraphs.tone: Thinking about "forever" makes Jack dizzy. It is a big, strange idea.

paragraphs.context: Rocks of all sizes crash into the moon from outer space
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains meteorites.
paragraphs.simple: Big and small rocks fly through space and hit the moon. They are called meteorites. That is why the moon has so many craters.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to stand. But his suit was too bulky
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack can't get up because of his big spacesuit.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's spacesuit is so big and stiff that he can't stand up, and he can't even turn over.
paragraphs.tone: This is scary: Jack is stuck, and their air is running out.

paragraphs.context: Hi,” she said. “We come in peace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie greets the strange spaceman in a friendly way.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says hello and tells the spaceman they are friends.

background.note: A famous line in films about meeting aliens. It also matches the words on the moon sign: "We came in peace".

paragraphs.context: That’s a jet pack!” said Jack
paragraphs.mainIdea: The spaceman flies with a jet pack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has seen pictures of future astronauts flying with jet packs. A jet pack is like a very small spaceship you wear on your back.

background.note: A real astronaut first flew free in space with a kind of jet pack in 1984.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie took long, floating steps toward the moon base
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hurry back to the base before their air runs out.
paragraphs.simple: They take big, slow steps back to the base. Jack holds his breath, as if he were swimming under water, to save air.

paragraphs.context: You know how you draw a constellation
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has an idea from the stars.
paragraphs.simple: To draw a group of stars, you join the stars with lines. Jack wants to "join" the four M things in the same way.

background.note: A group of stars that makes a shape in the sky, like the Big Dipper.

paragraphs.context: Jack touched each M thing in turn
paragraphs.mainIdea: They say the names of the four M things like a magic chant.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touches the moonstone, the mango, the mammoth bone and the mouse one by one, and says their names.
paragraphs.tone: All four words start with "M", so the chant sounds like a magic spell. The book writes "mango,mammoth" without a space; read it as "mango, mammoth".

paragraphs.context: And Morgan le Fay stood before Jack and Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: The spell is broken and Morgan is back.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly Morgan le Fay is standing in front of them. Peanut the mouse was really Morgan!
paragraphs.tone: This is the big surprise of the four books.

paragraphs.context: To break the spell, we had to be on the moon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan explains how the spell worked.
paragraphs.simple: The spell could only be broken on the moon. Jack and Annie could have broken it as soon as they arrived.

paragraphs.context: The same way you had a talk with the ninja master
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers friends who could talk to Peanut.
paragraphs.simple: In the last three books, a ninja master, a monkey and a sorcerer seemed to understand Peanut. Jack asks if Morgan "talked" with them in the same way.

paragraphs.context: Certain wise ones understand the language of little creatures
paragraphs.mainIdea: Some wise people and animals can understand small animals.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says that some wise beings can understand what small animals say.
paragraphs.tone: Morgan doesn't answer directly. She sounds a little mysterious.

paragraphs.context: Merlin!” said Jack. “The greatest magician
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merlin is the one who put the spell on Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows Merlin as the most famous magician in the King Arthur stories.

background.note: A great magician in the old British stories about King Arthur. He and Morgan le Fay are often rivals.

paragraphs.context: A bit of moondust still on you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan thanks Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan brushes moondust from Jack and thanks him because he loves to learn.

paragraphs.context: Morgan tugged on one of Annie’s braids
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan thanks Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan pulls Annie's hair kindly and thanks her because she believes that impossible things can happen.
paragraphs.tone: Jack and Annie are different: Jack loves facts, Annie believes in magic. Morgan thanks each of them for what they are good at.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. Home was Earth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is happy to go home to the Earth.
paragraphs.simple: After the gray, empty moon, Jack sees how wonderful the Earth is: bright, full of color, full of life and always changing.

paragraphs.context: Anything can happen,” said Morgan
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan says the universe is full of wonderful things.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells Jack that there are many amazing things in the universe, even things he can't explain.
paragraphs.tone: Morgan gently teases Jack, who always wants proof.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. The ladder was gone
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is gone.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack opens his eyes, the ladder and the tree house have disappeared. Only moonlight is left in the tree.
paragraphs.tone: A quiet, magical ending to the trip.

paragraphs.context: Wrong,” said Jack. “There’s no proof that aliens exist
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie disagree about the moon man.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the moon man was an alien. Jack says nobody has proved that aliens are real. Annie reminds him that they were in the future.

background.note: Living things from another planet, not from Earth.

paragraphs.context: Morgan’s words came back to him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers what Morgan said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks about Morgan's words: the universe is full of wonders. Maybe Annie is right.
paragraphs.tone: The book ends with a question, so the reader can decide.

sentences.context: She traveled through time and space, gathering books for her library
sentences.simple: She went to different times and places, and she collected books for her library.
sentences.main: She traveled through time and space.

parts.text: She traveled through time and space
parts.meaning: She went to other times and other places

parts.text: gathering books for her library
parts.job: What she did on her trips.
parts.meaning: and she collected books for her library.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part after the comma tells you what she did while she traveled.

sentences.context: Jack and Annie set out in the magic tree house to find four special things that would free her
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie started a trip in the tree house. They wanted to find four special things to make Morgan free.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie set out.

parts.text: Jack and Annie set out
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie started a trip

parts.text: in the magic tree house
parts.meaning: in the magic tree house

parts.text: to find four special things
parts.meaning: to look for four special things

parts.text: that would free her
parts.meaning: which could make Morgan free.

sentences.grammar: "Set out" means "start a trip". "That would free her" tells you what the four things can do.

sentences.context: With the help of a mouse named Peanut, Jack and Annie found the first thing in old Japan
sentences.simple: A mouse called Peanut helped them. They found the first thing in old Japan, the second in the rain forest and the third in the Ice Age.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie found the first thing in old Japan.

parts.text: With the help of a mouse named Peanut
parts.meaning: A mouse called Peanut helped them.

parts.text: Jack and Annie found the first thing in old Japan
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie found the first thing in Japan long ago,

parts.text: the second in the Amazon rain forest
parts.meaning: they found the second thing in the Amazon rain forest,

parts.text: and the third in the Ice Age
parts.meaning: and they found the third thing in the Ice Age.

sentences.grammar: The words "found ... thing" are not repeated in the last two parts. You add them in your head: "(found) the second (thing) in the Amazon rain forest".

sentences.context: No time will have passed
sentences.simple: When we come back, the time here will be the same as when we left.
sentences.main: No time will have passed.

parts.text: No time will have passed
parts.meaning: The clock will not move while we are away.

sentences.grammar: "Will have passed" looks at the future from a later time: when they come back, no time will be gone.

sentences.context: It shone on the three M things that rested on the M
sentences.simple: The moonlight fell on the three M things that were on the letter M: a moonstone, a mango and a mammoth bone.
sentences.main: It shone on the three M things.

parts.text: It shone on the three M things
parts.job: Main part: the moonlight lit up the things.
parts.meaning: The moonlight fell on the three things that start with M

parts.text: that rested on the M:
parts.meaning: that were lying on the letter M.

parts.text: a moonstone from the time of the ninjas
parts.meaning: They were a moonstone from the ninja trip,

parts.text: a mango from the Amazon rain forest
parts.meaning: a mango from the rain forest

parts.text: and a mammoth bone from the Ice Age
parts.meaning: and a mammoth bone from the Ice Age.

sentences.grammar: The colon (:) means "here is the list". "Shone" is the past of "shine". "Rested on" here means "lay on".

sentences.context: Not only that, we’d boil to death if it was day and freeze to death if it was night
sentences.simple: Also, we would die from heat in the daytime and die from cold at night.
sentences.main: We’d boil to death.

parts.text: Not only that
parts.meaning: And there is more:

parts.text: we’d boil to death if it was day
parts.meaning: we would die because it is too hot in the daytime

parts.text: and freeze to death if it was night
parts.meaning: and we would die because it is too cold at night.

sentences.grammar: "We'd" means "we would". It talks about what would happen if they went. "Boil to death" and "freeze to death" mean "die from heat" and "die from cold".

sentences.context: The top of the dome slides open to let spacecrafts enter and leave
sentences.simple: The top of the round roof opens so spaceships can come in and go out.
sentences.main: The top of the dome slides open.

parts.text: The top of the dome slides open
parts.meaning: The top of the round roof moves to the side and opens

parts.text: to let spacecrafts enter and leave
parts.meaning: so that spaceships can come in and go out.

sentences.grammar: "Let" + thing + action means "allow it to do something". Usually the plural is "spacecraft" (no -s), but this book writes "spacecrafts".

sentences.context: So this book was written after that! Which means this book is from the future
sentences.simple: So the book was written after 2031, and that means it comes from the future.
sentences.main: This book was written after that.

parts.text: So this book was written after that!
parts.meaning: So someone wrote this book after 2031!

parts.text: Which means this book is from the future
parts.meaning: That means the book comes from the future!

sentences.grammar: "Which means" starts a new sentence here, as people do when they talk. It means "and that shows...".

sentences.context: Morgan must have gone forward in time to borrow it from a future library
sentences.simple: Morgan probably traveled to the future and borrowed the book from a library there.
sentences.main: Morgan must have gone forward in time.

parts.text: Morgan must have gone forward in time
parts.meaning: I am sure Morgan traveled to the future

parts.text: to borrow it from a future library
parts.meaning: to borrow the book from a library in the future.

sentences.grammar: "Must have gone" is a strong guess about the past: "I'm almost sure she went".

sentences.context: Air and temperature controls make breathing possible
sentences.simple: Machines control the air and the heat, so people can breathe.
sentences.main: Controls make breathing possible.

parts.text: Air and temperature controls
parts.meaning: Machines that control the air and how hot or cold it is

parts.text: make breathing possible
parts.meaning: make it possible for people to breathe.

sentences.grammar: "Make" + thing + "possible" means "help it happen".

sentences.context: No air protects the moon from the sun’s rays, so daytime heat reaches 260 degrees
sentences.simple: There is no air to keep the sun's strong light away from the moon, so in the daytime it gets as hot as 260 degrees.
sentences.main: No air protects the moon.

parts.text: No air protects the moon from the sun’s rays
parts.meaning: There is no air to keep the sun's light away from the moon,

parts.text: so daytime heat reaches 260 degrees
parts.meaning: so in the daytime it gets as hot as 260 degrees.

sentences.grammar: "No air protects..." is a short way to say "There is no air to protect...". "So" shows the result.

sentences.context: Moon scientists wear spacesuits, which have controls to keep them from getting too hot or too cold
sentences.simple: Scientists on the moon wear spacesuits. The suits have controls that stop them from getting too hot or too cold.
sentences.main: Moon scientists wear spacesuits.

parts.text: Moon scientists wear spacesuits
parts.meaning: Scientists on the moon wear spacesuits

parts.text: which have controls
parts.meaning: and the suits have controls

parts.text: to keep them from getting too hot or too cold
parts.meaning: that stop them from getting too hot or too cold.

sentences.grammar: "Keep someone from doing something" means "stop it from happening".

sentences.context: So footprints will never wear away naturally, not even in a billion years
sentences.simple: So nothing in nature will ever wipe away the footprints, even after a billion years.
sentences.main: Footprints will never wear away.

parts.text: So footprints will never wear away naturally
parts.meaning: So footprints will never disappear by themselves,

parts.text: not even in a billion years
parts.meaning: even after a very, very long time.

sentences.grammar: "Wear away" means "slowly disappear". "Not even" makes the idea stronger.

sentences.context: If you weigh 60 pounds on Earth, you would only weigh 10 pounds on the moon
sentences.simple: Someone who is 60 pounds (27 kg) on Earth is only 10 pounds (4.5 kg) on the moon.
sentences.main: You would only weigh 10 pounds on the moon.

parts.text: If you weigh 60 pounds on Earth
parts.meaning: If you are 60 pounds (about 27 kilograms) on Earth,

parts.text: you would only weigh 10 pounds on the moon
parts.meaning: you are only 10 pounds (about 4.5 kilograms) on the moon.

sentences.grammar: "If ... would" tells what happens in a certain case. "Pounds" here is a unit of weight, not money.

sentences.context: The wide wheels kept it from sinking into the deep dust
sentences.simple: The wide wheels stopped the buggy from going down into the soft dust.
sentences.main: The wide wheels kept it from sinking.

parts.text: The wide wheels kept it
parts.meaning: The wide wheels stopped the buggy

parts.text: from sinking into the deep dust
parts.meaning: from going down into the deep dust.

sentences.grammar: "Keep something from doing something" means "stop it from doing it". "It" is the buggy.

sentences.context: But now, at least, he could take a good look at the moon
sentences.simple: But now the buggy was slower, so Jack could finally look at the moon carefully.
sentences.main: He could take a good look at the moon.

parts.text: But now, at least
parts.job: Something good in a hard time.
parts.meaning: But now one thing was better:

parts.text: he could take a good look at the moon
parts.meaning: he could look at the moon carefully.

sentences.grammar: "At least" points to one good thing in a bad situation. "Take a good look" means "look carefully".

sentences.context: He had never been to such a colorless, barren place
sentences.simple: Jack had never visited a place with no color and nothing growing.
sentences.main: He had never been to such a place.

parts.text: He had never been
parts.meaning: Jack had never visited

parts.text: to such a colorless, barren place
parts.meaning: a place so gray and empty, where nothing grows.

sentences.grammar: "Had never been to" means "had never visited". "Such a" makes the words after it stronger.

sentences.context: It would be there forever, unless someone moved it
sentences.simple: The notebook will stay there forever if nobody moves it.
sentences.main: It would be there forever.

parts.text: It would be there forever
parts.meaning: The notebook will stay there forever,

parts.text: unless someone moved it
parts.meaning: if nobody moves it.

sentences.grammar: "Unless" means "if not". "It" is the notebook with their names.

sentences.context: It was more than twice as tall as she was
sentences.simple: The rock was more than two times taller than Annie.
sentences.main: It was tall.

parts.text: It was more than twice as tall
parts.meaning: The rock was more than two times as high

parts.text: as she was
parts.meaning: as Annie.

sentences.grammar: "Twice as tall as" means "two times as tall as". "It" is the giant rock.

sentences.context: Jack held his breath as if he were underwater
sentences.simple: Jack stopped breathing for a while, like someone swimming under water.
sentences.main: Jack held his breath.

parts.text: Jack held his breath
parts.meaning: Jack stopped breathing for a short time

parts.text: as if he were underwater
parts.meaning: like someone under water.

sentences.grammar: "As if he were" talks about something not real: he was not really under water. We use "were" (not "was") after "as if" in careful English.

sentences.context: It was great to be free—even if he no longer felt as light as a feather
sentences.simple: Jack was glad to be out of the heavy suit, even though he did not feel super light any more.
sentences.main: It was great to be free.

parts.text: It was great to be free
parts.meaning: Jack loved being out of the spacesuit

parts.text: even if he no longer felt as light as a feather
parts.meaning: though he did not feel very light any more.

sentences.grammar: "Even if" here means "even though". "No longer" means "not any more". The dash (—) adds a small extra thought.

sentences.context: You could have broken it the minute we arrived
sentences.simple: You were able to break the spell as soon as we got to the moon.
sentences.main: You could have broken it.

parts.text: You could have broken it
parts.meaning: You were able to break the spell

parts.text: the minute we arrived
parts.meaning: as soon as we got here.

sentences.grammar: "Could have broken" means it was possible, but they didn't do it then. "The minute" means "as soon as".

sentences.context: Certain wise ones understand the language of little creatures
sentences.simple: Some wise people or animals can understand what small animals say.
sentences.main: Certain wise ones understand the language.

parts.text: Certain wise ones
parts.meaning: Some wise beings

parts.text: understand the language of little creatures
parts.meaning: can understand what small animals say.

sentences.grammar: "Ones" stands for people or animals. "Certain" here means "some special", not "sure".

sentences.context: Home was Earth—that bright, colorful world where everything was alive and always changing
sentences.simple: Jack's home was the Earth, a bright and colorful world full of life that is always changing.
sentences.main: Home was Earth.

parts.text: Home was Earth
parts.meaning: Jack's home was the Earth

parts.text: —that bright, colorful world
parts.meaning: that bright world with many colors,

parts.text: where everything was alive and always changing
parts.meaning: where everything lives and keeps changing.

sentences.grammar: The dash (—) adds more about "Earth". "Where" starts a part that tells about the world.

sentences.context: Where the tree house had been was only moonlight now
sentences.simple: Now there was only moonlight in the place where the tree house was before.
sentences.main: Where the tree house had been was only moonlight.

parts.text: Where the tree house had been
parts.meaning: In the place where the tree house was before,

parts.text: was only moonlight now
parts.meaning: there was only moonlight now.

sentences.grammar: The sentence starts with a place: "Where the tree house had been". "Had been" means it was there earlier, before now.

sentences.context: Could the moon man have come from another galaxy
sentences.simple: Was it possible that the moon man came from another galaxy?
sentences.main: Could the moon man have come from another galaxy?

parts.text: Could the moon man have come
parts.meaning: Is it possible that the moon man came

parts.text: from another galaxy
parts.meaning: from a different group of stars far away?

sentences.grammar: "Could ... have come" asks if something was possible in the past.
